summary: The return path (loans.service) and the reservation-expiry cron correctly serialize per-book hold promotion on the SAME advisory-lock key (book:<bookId>) — that pairing is sound. But the rest of the promotion machinery is NOT mutually exclusive: placeHold/import lock on a DIFFERENT key (reservation:<bookId>), and the cancel/expire admin path (resolveReservation → promoteNextHoldInTx) takes NO advisory lock at all AND promotes the queue head with an unconditional update (no status CAS), unlike every parallel implementation which uses a status='queued' compare-and-swap. A concurrent return-vs-cancel (or placeHold-vs-cancel) on the same book can therefore both promote, and the lock-free path clobbers the CAS-protected promotion, stranding a physical copy in 'reserved' with no reservation pointing at it — exactly the "copy stranded in reserved forever" failure. Two further real issues: (1) the offline circulation queue has no entry age-limit while the server idempotency record expires after 24h, opening a double-apply window for an action that actually committed before the device went offline for >24h (renew is the clean double-apply — it re-extends and re-increments renewedCount); (2) renew checks for a blocking hold outside any transaction/lock, so a hold placed in the check→update window is missed and the loan renews past it. Fine accrual is sound (single-outstanding-per-loan index + status-guarded upserts; floor-of-24h day count is intentional and matches the return path). Unit tests mock advisory locks as no-ops, so none of the lock-key / missing-CAS issues are caught by the existing suite — consistent with the audit lesson that static/test green masked a runtime concurrency hole.

findings.title: Hold promotion is not mutually exclusive across paths: cancel/expire takes no advisory lock and uses an unconditional (non-CAS) update, stranding a copy in 'reserved'
findings.evidence: The four promotion code paths use THREE different (non-overlapping) lock regimes. loans.service.returnLoan: `pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtextextended('book:${loan.copy.bookId}',0))` then promotes with a CAS: `tx.reservation.updateMany({ where: { id: head.id, status: 'queued' }, ... })`. reservation-expiry.job uses the SAME `book:${r.bookId}` key + CAS `updateMany({ where: { id: next.id, status: 'queued' } })` — these two correctly exclude each other. BUT placeHold locks a DIFFERENT key `reservation:${input.bookId}` (line 189), and resolveReservation (cancel via DELETE /reservations/:id, and admin/cron expire via POST /reservations/:id/expire) takes NO advisory lock anywhere in its `client.$transaction` (lines 316-359) and promotes via promoteNextHoldInTx, whose head update is UNCONDITIONAL: `await tx.reservation.update({ where: { id: head.id }, data: { status: 'ready', fulfilledByCopyId: candidateCopyId, ... } })` (lines 493-502) — no `status: 'queued'` guard. Concrete race (all normal librarian/cron actions): book has queued head H and a ready hold R holding copy C1. Thread A returnLoan(C2) acquires book: lock, CAS-promotes H, reserves C2. Thread B cancel(R) takes no lock, frees C1, selects the same H as head, then its unconditional update re-points H.fulfilledByCopyId to C1 (clobbering A's promotion). C2 was flipped to 'reserved' by A but no reservation now references it → permanently stranded copy. The B-vs-A pair shares no lock so they interleave freely under READ COMMITTED.
findings.impact: Data integrity / unrecoverable corruption on the running product: a physical copy can be stranded in 'reserved' with no reservation pointing at it (un-lendable until a human notices and manually fixes the status), and the promoted patron's hold can be silently re-pointed to a different copy. The queuePosition rebalance also runs twice, potentially leaving the queue inconsistent. Reachable through ordinary concurrent return + cancel/expire on a busy desk.
findings.fix: Make every per-book promotion path take the SAME advisory lock key (standardize on `book:${bookId}`) at the top of its transaction — including resolveReservation (cancel/expire) and placeHold/import (currently `reservation:${bookId}`). Additionally, change promoteNextHoldInTx's head promotion from `tx.reservation.update({ where: { id: head.id } })` to a CAS `tx.reservation.updateMany({ where: { id: head.id, status: 'queued' }, ... })` and bail (release the just-claimed copy) when count===0, matching loans.service and the expiry job.

adversarial.reason:
Independently confirmed. The cancel/expire path (reservations.service.ts resolveReservation, lines 283-364) wraps its work in client.$transaction (lines 316-359) with NO pg_advisory_xact_lock anywhere, and delegates promotion to promoteNextHoldInTx, whose head update at lines 493-502 is `tx.reservation.update({ where: { id: head.id }, data: { status:'ready', fulfilledByCopyId: candidateCopyId, ... } })` — unconditional, no `status:'queued'` CAS guard. The other three promotion paths all guard: loans.service.ts returnLoan (line 418) takes `book:${bookId}` advisory lock + CAS `updateMany({ where:{ id:head.id, status:'queued' } })` (line 434); reservation-expiry.job.ts (line 112) takes the SAME `book:${bookId}` lock + CAS at line 165; placeHold (line 189) takes `reservation:${bookId}` (a different key) but is internally safe via its liveCount-under-lock check. So cancel/expire shares no lock with the return/expiry paths.

Race verified under READ COMMITTED: book has queued head H + ready hold R holding copy C1. Thread A returnLoan(C2) holds the book: lock, CAS-promotes H to ready with fulfilledByCopyId=C2 and flips C2 on_loan→reserved. Thread B cancel(R) takes no lock; its promoteNextHoldInTx does a plain findFirst that can read H as still 'queued' before A commits, then issues an unconditional UPDATE WHERE id=H which blocks on A's row lock; after A commits, B's update does NOT re-check status (no CAS) and clobbers H.fulfilledByCopyId back to C1, succeeding because B freed C1 to 'available' earlier in its own tx so B's copy-claim CAS passes. Net result: C2 was flipped to 'reserved' by A but no reservation now references it → a physical copy permanently stranded in 'reserved' (un-lendable until manual repair), and the promoted patron's hold is silently re-pointed to a different copy. The CAS guard present in the other two paths would, after unblocking, see status='ready' and update 0 rows, bailing safely — which is exactly what's missing here. The duplicated queuePosition rebalance also runs in both txns.

Severity high (not critical) is appropriate: it is genuine data-integrity corruption on the running product reachable via ordinary concurrent return + cancel/expire at a busy desk, but it requires a specific concurrent interleaving (a precondition/timing window) rather than occurring on every operation, and the damage is a single stranded copy that a human can manually correct rather than unbounded/cascading corruption. The proposed fix (standardize on `book:${bookId}` lock across resolveReservation/placeHold and convert promoteNextHoldInTx's head update to a CAS updateMany that releases the claimed copy on count===0) is correct and matches the already-proven pattern in the sibling paths.

findings.title: Offline queue has no entry age-limit but server idempotency results expire after 24h, opening a double-apply window (renew re-extends + re-increments)
findings.evidence: offline-queue stores entries keyed by id with `createdAt` used ONLY for sort (`.sort((a,b)=>a.createdAt-b.createdAt)`); there is no age-based pruning and MAX_REPLAY_ATTEMPTS=6 counts only 5xx, not staleness. The server's idempotency record lives for `RESULT_TTL_SEC = 24*60*60`. Comment in offline-queue.ts claims safety 'rests on idempotency keys ... even if the original request had actually reached the server before the connection dropped' — but that guarantee evaporates once the 24h Redis record expires. Sequence: original POST commits server-side, response is lost on a dropped connection, device stays offline >24h; on reconnect OfflineQueueProvider.flush re-POSTs with the same Idempotency-Key, the interceptor's SETNX now succeeds (idem:<tenant>:<method>:<path>:<key> is gone), and `next.handle()` re-runs the operation. For renew this is a clean double-apply: LoansService.renew re-reads the (still-active) loan and its CAS `updateMany({ where: { id, status:'active', renewedCount: loan.renewedCount } })` passes on the fresh state, extending dueAt and incrementing renewedCount a SECOND time. (checkout is caught by loans_one_active_per_copy; most returns by the on_loan status CAS — renew is the unprotected one.)
findings.impact: A queued circulation action that already succeeded can be applied twice after a >24h offline gap. Renew double-extends the due date and over-counts renewals past maxRenewals; an over-billed/under-tracked loan results. Precondition-heavy (lost response + >24h offline) but fully silent — the librarian sees a 'synced' toast.
findings.fix: Either (a) cap offline-queue entry age (drop entries older than RESULT_TTL_SEC on flush and warn the librarian to re-verify), keeping it strictly below the server TTL; or (b) make the server idempotency RESULT_TTL_SEC effectively unbounded for these routes / persist the dedup record durably (DB) rather than only in Redis; and add a renewedCount/dueAt-aware guard so a stale renew replay is a no-op.

findings.title: Renew checks for a blocking hold outside any transaction/lock — a hold placed in the check→update window lets the loan renew past it
findings.evidence: renew is the only state-changing loan op with NO `client.$transaction` and no advisory lock. It reads `const queuedHold = await client.reservation.findFirst({ where: { bookId: loan.copy.bookId, status: { in: ['queued','ready'] } } })` (lines 612-615) and refuses if found, then later issues a separate `client.loan.updateMany(... renewedCount CAS ...)` (lines 632-635). Between the read and the write a concurrent placeHold (which locks only `reservation:${bookId}`, a different namespace) can insert a queued hold; renew has already passed its 'no hold waiting' check and proceeds to extend dueAt. The renewedCount CAS protects against double-renew but does nothing about a hold that appeared after the hold-check.
findings.impact: A member can renew and keep a book even though someone just got in line for it, contrary to the documented policy ('you can't renew while there's an active hold'). Self-correcting over time (the hold is promoted on the next return/expiry) so no corruption — purely a fairness/policy violation in a narrow race window.
findings.fix: Wrap the hold-check and the renew CAS in a single transaction that first takes the per-book advisory lock (same `book:${bookId}` key as the promotion paths), so a concurrent placeHold serializes against the renew decision.

findings.title: Idempotency replay does not re-assert the original HTTP status code (cosmetic; not a correctness bug)
findings.evidence: On a winning claim the interceptor stores only `{ body }` (line 84) and on replay returns `of(parsed.body)` (line 102), letting Nest apply the ROUTE's default status to the replay rather than the original response's status. For these routes all success responses are 200/201 so the replayed status matches; and the same-key/different-body case correctly replays the original result (true idempotency-key semantics, not a body-hash mismatch error) which is acceptable for a trusted librarian client. Noted only because a future route returning a dynamic status would replay the wrong code.
findings.impact: None today — all four circulation routes return a fixed success status, so replays are correct. Latent risk if a variable-status route is later decorated with this interceptor.
findings.fix: Optionally persist and restore the original status code alongside the body on replay; document that the interceptor assumes a fixed success status per route.
